title: Interview: Firefox's chief on why he hopes a redesign will help win users from Chrome
gist: Mozilla's head of Firefox Ajit Varma says the Firefox 157 redesign aims to win mainstream users on product merit, not just open-web values, by exploiting 'consideration moments' such as EU choice screens, Chrome's Manifest V2 deprecation and AI bloat, while investing heavily in enterprise tools and using AI coding to boost velocity. Firefox remains financially dependent on Google search revenue, spends under 10% of engineering on AI, and cannot ship Gecko on iOS without global Apple rules; Forrester's Paddy Harrington is skeptical of its enterprise and AI-coding advantages.

themes.theme: Firefox's market position and core challenge

insights.claim: Forrester analyst Paddy Harrington says Firefox's biggest barrier to adoption is simply that it is not Chrome, noting people download Chrome even though Safari and Edge are built into leading operating systems.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Chrome's default-like brand power remains a durable moat for Google.
insights.quote: “The biggest is they’re not Chrome,” he replied.
insights.locator: Firefox’s interface has recently felt

insights.claim: Google-led Chromium dominates the web, powering both majority-share Chrome and most competitors including Microsoft Edge, leaving Gecko-based Firefox as the main Chromium-free alternative.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Engine consolidation gives Google outsized influence over web standards and extensions.
insights.locator: That said, for many of the people

insights.claim: Mozilla gets the majority of its revenue from a deal making Google search Firefox's default, so Firefox seeks web independence while remaining financially dependent on its dominant competitor.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Any disruption to Google's search payments (e.g. via antitrust remedies) is an existential risk to Mozilla.
insights.quote: For now, Firefox seeks independence for the web while remaining financially dependent on its dominant competitor.
insights.locator: Firefox, which is built on the open source Gecko

insights.claim: Varma says most mainstream users do not understand the difference between Chromium, Blink, Chrome and Gecko, or even between a search engine and a browser, so Firefox must win on how enjoyable the browser feels.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Values-based positioning has a ceiling; mass-market share requires product differentiation.
insights.quote: A lot of people actually don’t even really know what the difference is between a search engine and a browser, and it’s all conflated.
insights.locator: When we talk to a lot of users

insights.claim: Varma argues owning the entire Gecko stack lets Firefox make bolder changes than Chromium forks, which tend to look similar because superficial changes are easier than deep ones.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Engine ownership could be a differentiation lever versus Chromium-based rivals.
insights.quote: But we get an advantage by owning the entire stack. We can actually make bolder changes.
insights.locator: And that’s where we do have an opportunity

insights.claim: Varma says the biggest predictor of what browser someone uses is what they used the previous month, making consideration the main barrier to switching.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Browser share is sticky, so default placement and switching triggers dominate market dynamics.
insights.quote: The biggest indicator, though, of what browser someone uses is actually, what browser did they use last month?
insights.locator: The biggest indicator, though

insights.claim: Firefox has seen significant growth since EU Digital Markets Act mobile browser choice screens were implemented.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Regulatory choice screens measurably shift share away from platform defaults, a template for other markets.
insights.quote: We see a lot of growth in Firefox since these choice screens were implemented
insights.locator: We do see that when people have a moment

insights.claim: Varma says Chrome's deprecation of Manifest V2 was clearly driven by ad blockers, and Firefox's continued support produced a big surge of users after all Chromium browsers dropped it.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Google's ad-business incentives can create switching opportunities for rivals.
insights.quote: And it’s very clearly because of ad blockers. That was the reason to deprecate it.
insights.locator: So some examples—Chrome went through

insights.claim: Varma argues major browsers care more about AI adoption than browsing experience, citing Edge becoming a Copilot app and Gemini's forceful Chrome integration, while users mainly use ChatGPT and Claude.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Platform-owner AI assistants may not win browser-level AI usage despite default placement.
insights.quote: but neither Copilot nor Gemini are the main AI that people use. People use ChatGPT, people use Claude.
insights.locator: Also, with AI controls

insights.claim: Firefox's strategy for the next year centers on creating more consideration moments, such as top-level AI controls and customization, that prompt users to rethink their browser.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Indicates where Firefox will concentrate product effort to gain share.
insights.locator: So we built AI controls

insights.claim: Varma says enterprise and school tools such as data loss prevention, manageability and controls have been Firefox's biggest new area of investment over the last 12 months, with a fairly sizable team.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Firefox is targeting managed-browser deployments where default decisions are made by IT.
insights.locator: One of the biggest new investments

insights.claim: Varma reports rising interest from companies in Europe and Asia seeking browsers not controlled by governments they see as antagonistic, drawn by Firefox's open source nature.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Digital sovereignty demand may erode US Big Tech's software position in Europe and Asia.
insights.locator: The other thing that we’re seeing

insights.claim: Harrington says Firefox's enterprise comeback will not be easy and would need to truly wow IT decision makers, with the clearest opening among European businesses moving away from Microsoft and Google.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: European de-risking from US platforms is a real but narrow opening for alternatives.
insights.quote: “I’d certainly love to see them come back with new things that expands them in the enterprise, but it’s not going to be easy, and they would have to truly wow IT decision makers,”
insights.locator: Given Varma’s statement

insights.claim: Varma says AI tools have helped Firefox overcome historically slow decision-making and greatly increase development velocity over the past year and a half.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: AI coding tools may let smaller software firms compete with larger incumbents.
insights.quote: And part of this is made possible by AI tools, to be honest with you.
insights.locator: We are trying to do all of the above

insights.claim: Varma says that with AI, the bottleneck for a smaller company is no longer code creation but code review, and hopes AI tools get commoditized so costs don't rise.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Code review and AI tool pricing become the key constraints on software productivity gains.
insights.quote: the bottleneck is not code creation anymore. We can create tons of code. It’s actually code review.
insights.locator: I don’t know how that’ll play out

insights.claim: Harrington counters that AI coding is not a de facto advantage for smaller firms because Apple, Google and Microsoft surely use it too; the question is how they use it differently.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: AI productivity gains may not shift competitive balance if incumbents adopt equally.
insights.quote: “If large companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft aren’t using AI within their dev processes, then I’ll eat my hat, as the old saying goes,”
insights.locator: As Varma tells it

insights.claim: Varma says daily AI tool usage in browsers is still a small minority of browser usage, though productivity uses like translation, summarization and tab grouping are emerging.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: In-browser AI demand remains early, tempering expectations for AI-driven browser monetization.
insights.quote: The usage of AI is still a minority compared to the overall browser usage.
insights.locator: The usage of AI is still a minority

insights.claim: Fewer than 10% of Firefox engineers work on AI; Mozilla uses open source and on-device models rather than building its own models or agents, and its biggest investment remains Gecko.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: A capital-light AI approach contrasts with VC-backed peers spending hundreds of millions.
insights.quote: the number of engineers that we have working on this versus all the other stuff is less than 10 percent of the overall engineering
insights.locator: I think that there’s probably speculation

insights.claim: Varma says AI will help with productivity browser use cases but the core browser will still be needed for entertainment, and 90% of Firefox's attention remains on core fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Suggests agentic AI will not fully displace traditional browsing.
insights.quote: Ninety percent of our attention is still very focused on those core fundamentals.
insights.locator: And then the other side of it

insights.claim: Varma acknowledges Mozilla's mistake 15 years ago of not investing in mobile apps early enough while focusing on desktop.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Firefox's weak mobile position limits its overall share, since mobile drives habits.
insights.quote: one of the mistakes that Mozilla made 15 years ago was, it didn’t invest in mobile apps early enough
insights.locator: That’s things like performance

insights.claim: Varma says shipping Gecko on iPhone in the EU and Japan only would require roughly doubling Firefox's iOS team, so Mozilla is pressing Apple and regulators for a single set of global rules.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Fragmented regional remedies blunt the competitive effect of regulations aimed at Apple.
insights.quote: would mean we would basically have to double the size of our iOS team
insights.locator: The biggest challenge for us

insights.claim: Varma says that in the short term LLMs are growing the overall search pie rather than pulling users from Google, with search and monetizable queries rising and user muscle memory for Google still strong.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Counters the narrative that AI chatbots are eroding Google Search revenue in the near term.
insights.quote: Search queries and monetizable queries are actually going up.
insights.locator: But in the short term, Google is doing really well

insights.claim: Varma says the more people use Firefox, the more negotiating power Mozilla has to create balance and protect the web.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Firefox's user share directly underpins its bargaining position with Google on search revenue.
insights.quote: The more people use Firefox, the more power I think we have to negotiate
insights.locator: So I don’t know how it’ll play out

insights.claim: The author concludes the redesign is a welcome start for mass-market appeal amid frustration with Big Tech, but Mozilla still faces a long road against better-resourced competitors.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Meaningful share gains for Firefox remain uncertain despite favorable regulatory tailwinds.
insights.quote: that’s a welcome start, but it’s not the finish line
insights.locator: Whatever the scope of the enterprise opportunity
